title: Physical Constraints on Latency and Energy Use in Biological and Artificial Information Processing
plain_title: How fast and how cheaply can brains and chips compute?
thesis: Brains and computers are both held back by the same physics, how far a signal must travel and how much heat it makes, and when you compare like with like a brain synapse is only about 71 times more energy efficient than a top graphics chip, not 100,000 times.
summary: The paper builds a table of 33 computing systems, from a single brain synapse and a squid nerve to Nvidia graphics chips, light-based chips and superconducting logic cooled to 4.2 kelvin, and records for each one how long a signal takes, how much power it uses and how many operations it gets per joule. It argues that signal delay is set by distance divided by speed (or distance squared for diffusion), that the famous Landauer heat limit does not affect single decisions, and that the energy gap between brains and chips is much smaller than usually claimed. It then adds side arguments about how brain energy use scales with neuron count and how brain mass scales with body mass. We recomputed the key ratios from the project's data files and the paper's own stated inputs.

claims.claim: A cortical synapse is about 71 times more energy efficient than a dense 16-bit operation on an Nvidia H100 chip.
claims.paper_value: 10¹⁴ events per joule divided by 1.41×10¹² operations per joule = 70.9 times
claims.source: cleaned_hardware_benchmarks.csv, synapse row divided by H100 dense row; the synapse value itself is taken from Attwell and Laughlin (2001), not measured here
claims.note: We divided the two rows and got 70.92; the arithmetic is right, but both inputs are literature numbers copied into the file, and a synaptic event and a 16-bit multiply are different kinds of operation, which the paper itself admits.

claims.claim: Superconducting AQFP logic still beats everything after paying a roughly 400-to-1 electricity penalty for cooling to 4.2 kelvin.
claims.paper_value: 7.14×10¹⁹ operations per joule at the core, 1.79×10¹⁷ after the 400 times cooling penalty; 1,790 times better than a synapse
claims.data_value: Carnot coefficient 0.0142, ideal cost 70.4 W per W, at 17.5% of ideal 402 W per W; 7.14×10¹⁹ / 402 = 1.78×10¹⁷; 1.79×10¹⁷ / 10¹⁴ = 1,790
claims.source: Recomputed the Carnot chain from 4.2 K and 300 K and the ratios from cleaned_hardware_benchmarks.csv rows for AQFP core, AQFP wall-plug and synapse
claims.note: Every step of the cooling-penalty arithmetic reproduces within rounding; the 1.4×10⁻²⁰ joules per switch is a single literature value for a laboratory circuit, not a working computer.

claims.claim: Cooled AQFP logic is five orders of magnitude (about 120,000 times) more efficient than the best room-temperature CMOS chip.
claims.data_value: 127,000 times against the H100 only; 11,800 times against the Apple M4 as printed in Table 1 (1.52×10¹³), 23,600 times against the M4 in the data file (7.6×10¹²), 39,800 times against the B200
claims.source: cleaned_hardware_benchmarks.csv: 1.79×10¹⁷ divided by each CMOS row's efficiency
claims.note: The factor 1.2×10⁵ only appears if the H100 (1.41×10¹² ops per joule) is called the best CMOS chip, but the paper's own table lists three CMOS chips that beat it, and against the best of them the gap is about 10⁴, four orders of magnitude, not five.

claims.claim: Table 1 reports the measured latency, power and efficiency of the electric fish pacemaker, the dragonfly interception neuron and the Apple M4 Neural Engine.
claims.paper_value: Fish: 1 mm, 0.16 microseconds, 10⁻⁸ W, 5×10¹⁰ ops per joule. Dragonfly: 12 mm, 4.5 m/s, 28 ms, 5×10⁻⁷ W, 8×10⁸ ops per joule. M4: 2.5 W, 2.11×10⁻¹⁰ s, 1.52×10¹³ ops per joule (15.2 TOPS/W)
claims.data_value: Fish: 2 mm, 1 millisecond, 2×10⁻⁷ W, 5×10⁹ ops per joule. Dragonfly: 4 mm, 4 m/s, 25 ms, 5×10⁻⁶ W, 8×10⁶ ops per joule. M4: 5 W, 4.44×10⁻¹⁰ s, 7.6×10¹² ops per joule (7.6 TOPS/W)
claims.source: cleaned_hardware_benchmarks.csv, the three rows for these systems, compared field by field with Table 1
claims.note: All three rows disagree with the data file: the fish latency differs 6,000-fold, the dragonfly efficiency 100-fold and the M4 efficiency 2-fold (the paper's 15.2 TOPS/W is 3.8×10¹³ ops per second divided by 2.5 W, while the file uses 5 W); the other 21 printed rows match the file.

claims.claim: Brain mass grows with body mass to the power 0.87 across the cleaned species catalog.
claims.data_value: 277 rows, slope 0.7955, intercept −1.963, R² 0.576, standard error 0.041 (all rows with positive masses); slope 0.83, R² 0.80 if the obvious non-animals are dropped
claims.source: cleaned_biological_species.csv, ordinary least squares of log10 brain mass on log10 body mass
claims.note: No subset we tried gives 0.8727 or R² 0.7362; the file has 277 rows, not the 195 species the authors' review notes describe, and it still contains entries such as Wikipedia, a starling flock and a penguin huddle with 'brain mass' larger than 'body mass'.

claims.claim: Brain power grows with neuron count to the power 0.86 rather than following the 0.75 body-mass law.
claims.data_value: not in the species file (it has no power column); the only project file with both brain power and neuron counts gives exponent 0.98 ± 0.05, R² 0.93 over 29 rows
claims.source: cleaned_biological_species.csv has no brain power column; neural_sensory_evolution_timeseries.csv, log10 brain watts against log10 neurons
claims.note: The paper says the exponent comes from 'our calibrated biological species dataset', but that dataset has no power numbers, and the one project table that does gives a slope near 1.0, not 0.86.

claims.claim: A budget of 500 picowatts per neuron predicts a human brain power of 18 to 22 watts.
claims.source: Arithmetic on the paper's own inputs
claims.note: Multiplying the paper's two numbers gives 43 W, about double the 20 W it claims to match; the 0.86 exponent is not applied in the sentence and no prefactor is given that would bring it down.

claims.claim: The 33 systems span 16 orders of magnitude in latency and 12 orders of magnitude in energy efficiency.
claims.data_value: 14.8 orders in latency (2.13×10⁻¹¹ s to 1.36×10⁴ s) and 14.2 orders in efficiency (4.35×10⁵ to 7.14×10¹⁹ ops per joule)
claims.source: cleaned_hardware_benchmarks.csv, min and max of total latency and of efficiency across all 33 rows
claims.note: Neither span matches the file; the 12-order efficiency span only appears if you use the 24 rows printed in Table 1, which omit the least efficient system (the blowfly reflex at 4.35×10⁵ ops per joule).

claims.claim: Neurotransmitter diffusion across a 20-nanometre synaptic gap takes about 200 microseconds.
claims.paper_value: about 200 microseconds, from L = 20 nm and D = 0.76 µm² per ms
claims.data_value: L² / 2D = (2×10⁻⁸ m)² / (2 × 7.6×10⁻¹⁰ m²/s) = 0.26 microseconds; the hardware file's synapse row nevertheless lists 200 microseconds of transport time
claims.source: Paper's own diffusion formula with the paper's own inputs; cleaned_hardware_benchmarks.csv synapse row
claims.note: The paper's formula and inputs give a quarter of a microsecond, about 760 times shorter than stated; 200 microseconds is roughly the whole synaptic delay (vesicle release plus receptor response), not the diffusion time, and Figure 1 plots the wrong value.

claims.claim: Surface bacteria use about 1 femtowatt per cell, 1,000 times more than deep-sediment bacteria at 1 attowatt, and this gap follows from first principles.
claims.paper_value: 10⁻¹⁵ W per cell versus 10⁻¹⁸ W per cell, a 1,000 times gap; surface value derived as 1.0×10⁻⁹ J divided by 1,800 s plus motility
claims.data_value: 1.0×10⁻⁹ J / 1,800 s = 5.6×10⁻¹³ W, about 560 times larger than the stated 10⁻¹⁵ W; the deep-sediment sum (1.2×10⁻¹⁹ + 8.8×10⁻¹⁹ = 1.0×10⁻¹⁸ W) does reproduce
claims.source: Arithmetic on the paper's own inputs; the project's hardware file lists the E. coli chemotaxis cluster at 10⁻¹⁵ W
claims.note: The derivation's first term alone is 560 times bigger than its own answer, so the 'first-principles' 1,000-fold gap does not follow from the numbers shown (they would give roughly 560,000-fold); the 1 femtowatt and 1 attowatt figures are literature values, not results of the derivation.

rationale.step: A signal cannot arrive faster than distance divided by speed (or distance squared over diffusion constant for diffusing molecules), so the slowest chain of steps sets the minimum decision time.
rationale.note: This is standard physics and the hardware file is built on it, but the paper's own examples break it: the electric fish latency of 0.16 microseconds in Table 1 is 300 times shorter than the 50 microseconds its 1 mm path at 20 m/s allows, and the synaptic-gap diffusion time is overstated 760-fold.

rationale.step: The Landauer heat cost of erasing a bit is irrelevant to how fast one decision can be made; it only limits how fast you can keep cycling once heat must be removed.
rationale.note: We reproduce 2.871×10⁻²¹ J at 300 K and 1.44×10⁻²² s for a 20 W brain; the argument is sound, though the text's 'twelve orders of magnitude below a millisecond' should be nineteen.

rationale.step: Compare like with like: an on-chip 16-bit operation against a synaptic event gives a gap of about 71 times, so the usual 100,000-fold gap is an artifact of comparing synapses with slow off-chip memory fetches.
rationale.note: The 71 reproduces, but both inputs are copied literature values, the two operations are admitted to be different things, and the paper's own 'artifact' comparison gives 20,000, not 100,000, so the claimed origin of the famous gap is not actually demonstrated.

rationale.step: Superconducting logic cooled to 4.2 kelvin is so efficient that even after a 400-fold electricity cost for refrigeration it beats both synapses and CMOS chips.
rationale.note: The cooling arithmetic is right and the 1,790-fold lead over a synapse follows, but the 'five orders of magnitude over the best CMOS' only holds against the H100; against the best CMOS chip in the paper's own table it is about four orders.

rationale.step: Brain energy follows neuron count (exponent 0.86), not the 0.75 body-mass law, and brain mass follows body mass with exponent 0.87 in the cleaned catalog.
rationale.note: Neither regression reproduces from the project files (we get 0.98 for power versus neurons and 0.80 for brain versus body with R² 0.58), and the worked human example gives 43 W, not the 18 to 22 W claimed.

conclusions.conclusion: When you compare a dense on-chip operation with a synaptic event, the brain's energy advantage over a modern GPU is about 71 times, not 100,000 times.
conclusions.note: The ratio is correctly computed from two literature values, but the paper does not show that the 100,000 figure comes from memory fetches (its own version of that comparison gives 20,000), and it never settles whether a synaptic event and a 16-bit multiply are comparable units.

conclusions.conclusion: Cryogenic superconducting logic, even charged 400 times for cooling, beats synapses by about 1,800 times and room-temperature CMOS by 100,000 times.
conclusions.note: The synapse comparison and the cooling penalty hold; the CMOS comparison is overstated by about a factor of ten because it uses the H100 rather than the more efficient CMOS chips in the same table.

conclusions.conclusion: Decision latency is set by signal travel distance and speed, with a square-law penalty only for diffusion, and the Landauer heat limit plays no role in single-decision speed.
conclusions.note: The physics and the Landauer arithmetic check out; the weak spots are specific example numbers (fish pacemaker, synaptic gap, Trichoplax) that disagree with the very formula being illustrated.

conclusions.conclusion: Brain power scales with neuron count to the 0.86 power and brain mass with body mass to the 0.87 power, so Kleiber's 0.75 law does not govern brains.
conclusions.note: Neither exponent can be recovered from the project data, the species file is still contaminated with non-animals, the human worked example is off by a factor of two, and the paper itself defers the proper analysis to a future Paper 2.

inconsistencies: Three rows of Table 1 (electric fish pacemaker, dragonfly neuron, Apple M4) disagree with the hardware data file by factors of 2 to 6,000, while the paper says the table was built from that file.

The electric fish entry gives a latency of 0.16 microseconds for a 1 mm path at 20 m/s, which is 300 times faster than the paper's own rule 'time is at least distance divided by speed' allows; 0.16 microseconds is the timing jitter reported in the source, not a latency.

The paper says the best room-temperature CMOS chip is beaten by 1.2×10⁵, using the H100 at 1.41×10¹² ops per joule, yet its own Table 1 lists the Apple M4 at 1.52×10¹³, the B200 at 4.5×10¹² and Cerebras at 3.23×10¹², all more efficient than the H100.
The abstract says the 100,000-fold gap is an artifact of comparing synapses with DRAM fetches, but the paper's own synapse-to-DRAM ratio is 20,000, five times smaller.
The abstract claims 16 orders of magnitude in latency and 12 in efficiency; the data file gives 14.8 and 14.2.
The synaptic-gap diffusion time is stated as 200 microseconds and plotted that way in Figure 1, but the paper's own formula with its own inputs gives 0.26 microseconds.
The 500 picowatt per neuron budget times 86 billion neurons is 43 W, not the 18 to 22 W the text says it predicts.
The surface-bacterium derivation's first term (10⁻⁹ J over 1,800 s) is 5.6×10⁻¹³ W, 560 times larger than the 10⁻¹⁵ W it is said to yield, so the 'derived' 1,000-fold gap does not follow.
The brain-body regression (slope 0.8727, R² 0.7362) does not reproduce from the cleaned species file (slope 0.80, R² 0.58, 277 rows), and the authors' own review notes say the file had 195 species.
The brain-power exponent 0.86 is attributed to the species dataset, which contains no power measurements at all.
The introduction says vacuum tubes switched six orders of magnitude faster than neurons and then quotes 10⁻⁶ s versus 10⁻³ s, which is three orders.
Section 3.2 says 1.44×10⁻²² s is twelve orders of magnitude below a 1 millisecond membrane time constant; the gap is nineteen orders.

Trichoplax is said to coordinate over 1 mm at 150 micrometres per second in 1.5 s; 1 mm divided by 150 micrometres per second is 6.7 s, and quoting a steady speed contradicts calling it pure diffusion.
The brain's share of body energy is said to span 'over three orders of magnitude' from 0.0008 to 0.25, which is a factor of 312, about 2.5 orders.
Songbird neuron density is given as 1.56×10⁸ per gram in Section 3.4.1 and 2.4×10⁸ per gram in Section 5.4.
The catalog is described throughout as 950 systems, 2,616 measurements and 1,275 sources, but the spreadsheet in the data folder holds 975 systems, 2,641 observation ids and about 1,300 sources.

The catalog numbers the paper attaches to the squid giant axon, the blue whale and modern humans point to a roundworm, an extinct small-bodied human species and no entry at all in the project's species file.

Table 1 is introduced as covering the 33 benchmark substrates but prints 24 rows, and Figure 1 plots systems (a transatlantic internet ping, historical vacuum-tube computers) that are not among the 33 in the data file.
bottom_line: A reader can rely on the core physics (signal delay is distance over speed, Landauer heat does not limit single decisions) and on the headline arithmetic: synapse over H100 is 71, cooled superconducting logic over synapse is about 1,800. Do not yet rely on the 'five orders over the best CMOS' claim (it is about four), on any of the brain-scaling exponents (neither reproduces from the project data), or on several worked examples whose own numbers do not multiply out.
